Each time we recall an event, we actually reconstruct it, and new information can slip into the reconstruction. In a famous experiment, participants watched a car accident. Those asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed' into each other reported higher speeds than those who heard the word 'hit.' A week later, the 'smashed' group even remembered seeing broken glass — glass that never existed. This is called the misinformation effect, and it has led many courts to treat eyewitness accounts with greater caution.

Their skin contains thousands of pigment sacs called chromatophores, each controlled by muscles and nerves, which expand or contract to change color in a fraction of a second. One hypothesis is that light-sensitive proteins in the skin itself allow the octopus to 'see' with its body. The debate is ongoing, but it reminds us that vision, in the broadest sense, need not be confined to eyes.

When we say 'Silk Road,' the singular is misleading. It was a shifting network of caravan routes linking China to the Mediterranean, and silk was only one of many goods. Paper, spices, glassware, and horses moved along it — but so did ideas. Buddhism traveled from India into China along these routes, and centuries later, technologies like papermaking moved west, reaching Europe through the Islamic world. Of course, the network also carried disease; many historians believe the plague of the fourteenth century followed trade routes into Europe. So the Silk Road is best understood not as a road at all, but as history's first great information superhighway — with all the benefits and risks that implies.

Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they support about a quarter of all marine species. The coral animal itself is nearly transparent; its brilliant colors come from microscopic algae living inside its tissues. The algae photosynthesize and share nutrients with the coral — a textbook case of mutualism. But this partnership is temperature-sensitive. When water warms by even one or two degrees for several weeks, corals expel their algae and turn bone white, a process called bleaching. Bleached corals are not dead, but they are starving, and if the heat persists they die. That's why marine biologists treat mass bleaching events as early warning systems for ocean warming.

How do we find planets orbiting stars light-years away, when the star outshines the planet a billion to one? Mostly, we don't look for the planet at all — we watch the star. In the transit method, we measure the star's brightness continuously; if a planet crosses in front, the light dips by a tiny, regular amount. The size of the dip tells us the planet's diameter, and the interval between dips gives its orbital period. The radial velocity method instead watches the star wobble: an orbiting planet tugs its star back and forth, shifting the starlight's color slightly toward blue, then red. Combining both methods yields the planet's density — and that tells us whether we're looking at a gas giant or a rocky world like our own.
